title: The milk left on the fire
hookLine: on the autumn full moon the flute calls, and the gopis go just as they are
carry: bhakti comes as it is, like the gopis
tomorrow: a king stops the story: how could this love be holy?

lines: THE MILK IS ON THE FIRE.
A FULL MOON OVER THE TREES.
cards: The milk is on the fire. Someone is halfway through milking a cow. Someone is serving food to her family.
Someone has a baby at her breast. It's an autumn night in Vraja, the moon full and coming up red over the trees, and every house is in the middle of something. Then, from the forest, the flute.
Not the daytime music the gopis talked about from a distance. This time, the Bhagavata says, the sound is calling them.

teach.h: EACH ONE GOES EXACTLY AS SHE IS.
teach.b: The text slows down and goes house by house. The women hear the flute and go, each one exactly as she is. The one milking leaves the cow.
The one boiling milk leaves the pot on the fire. The one cooking leaves the food unserved. The one feeding a child, the one eating her own dinner: all of them stand up and go.
Some were dressing, and they go with their ornaments in disarray. Husbands, fathers and brothers try to stop them; they don't turn around.

teach.h: SOME KEPT INSIDE GO IN MEDITATION.
teach.b: And some, the Bhagavata adds, were kept inside, and those women shut their eyes and went to him in meditation instead. Why linger on the half-finished jobs? Because the list is the point.
Nobody finishes anything or makes herself presentable first. And notice who these are: not sages, not priests, not scholars of the Veda.
Cowherd women with milk on the stove.

Yet Hindu tradition holds them up as the very picture of bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras, a short classic on devotion, points to the gopis of Vraja as its example. Devotional readers hear the soul answering God here.
It doesn't arrive polished or qualified. It comes as it is, and even the ones who can't leave the house reach him by remembering. The Bhagavata doesn't let the scene pass unexamined, though.
Right after this, the king who's listening stops the story with a hard question. That's tomorrow.

how: The opening of the rasa lila chapters, with the gopis leaving their work at the sound of the flute, is recited at katha and sung by Krishna devotees, and teachers of bhakti point to the gopis as devotion's model.

o: a warning that Kamsa's soldiers are near the village
a signal that the cows are loose in the forest
the sound that calls the gopis out, mid-task, at night

games.q: sam says real devotion is for priests and people who know all the texts. by tonight's story, what do you say?
o: he's right. the gopis were just fans.
the tradition's own model of bhakti is cowherd women who came as they were.
devotion only counts inside the temple.
games.why: the Narada Bhakti Sutras point to the gopis of Vraja as the example of bhakti: village women, mid-task, coming just as they were.

practice: Notice what you just set down to be here, a phone, a cup, a list, and leave it untidied. Then do what the women kept inside did: close your eyes and turn toward him.

If you pray, say one name, Krishna, Govinda, or the name of God you use, silently with each breath, and come just as you are, without fixing anything first. When the half-done things tug, notice the tug and come back to the name.
If you don't pray, rest your attention on someone you love, as you are, unfinished.

wordCard.voice: The flute. On the autumn night, the sound that calls the gopis out of their houses, mid-task, just as they are.

orig.note: Sanskrit: autumn, the season of the full-moon night when the flute calls.
